title: A Clock for the Orchard
premise: In 1917, Oscar Whitlock serves as driver and letter-reader for suffragist Edith Marlowe, memorizing the names in a ledger of women organizing against the war effort. When the army requisitions the town and seizes the ledger as evidence of sedition, Oscar—long invisible by design—becomes the only living record of the network. She must smuggle testimony, protect the women named within, and outmaneuver Captain Renshaw, who wants the ledger burned and the story rewritten. The book ends with Oscar testifying before a postwar inquiry, choosing love with fellow courier Nell over the safety of anonymity, and watching the truth enter the official record just ahead of the victors' historians.
about_author: Rafael Hartwell is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in regional county records. A Clock for the Orchard is their third novel, drawn from the marginalia of confiscated letters they were never supposed to read.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. We meet her reading letters aloud to illiterate townsfolk, quietly memorizing what she carries, and measuring her life in portable things. Emotional beat: the comfort—and cost—of being nobody.

chapters.title: Mrs. Marlowe's Ledger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Edith Marlowe entrusts Oscar with the ledger of the orchard network, names and routes and safehouses. Oscar resists the responsibility; Edith insists invisibility is a skill, not an identity. Beat: reluctant acceptance.

chapters.title: Nell at the Crossing
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On a delivery run she encounters Nell Ashby, a courier from a neighboring town, and the two trade coded phrases neither admits to knowing. Beat: first spark of connection, guarded on both sides.

chapters.title: Orders Come Down
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Captain Renshaw. The army announces requisition of the town; Renshaw arrives with a mandate to seize seditious materials. Beat: dread settling like weather.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. With hours' warning, the network scatters its papers. Oscar hides the ledger inside the clock housing of the orchard gatehouse. Beat: fear sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Requisition
chapters.summary: Renshaw's POV. Soldiers occupy the town; the Marlowe house is searched and the ledger is not found—but Renshaw notices Oscar's steady hands and files her away as a question. Beat: the hunter's patience.

chapters.title: A Town Under New Management
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Occupation life: curfews, billeted soldiers, neighbors informing on neighbors. Oscar delivers mail under supervision, reading less, remembering more. Beat: isolation and quiet defiance.

chapters.title: The Interrogation of Edith Marlowe
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Questioned without charge, Edith gives nothing but courtesy. Oscar waits outside, learning how power performs itself. Beat: admiration curdling into anger.

chapters.title: Two Roads Out of Town
chapters.summary: Oscar and Nell's POV alternating. The pair smuggle a witness list to a sympathetic printer two counties over, nearly caught at a checkpoint. Beat: trust forged under pressure; love admitted in a hayloft.

chapters.title: The Informer
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Someone in the network talks. A safehouse burns; a friend is taken. Oscar suspects the town clerk, whose son wears a uniform. Beat: paranoia fracturing the found family.

chapters.title: Renshaw's Offer
chapters.summary: Renshaw's POV. He offers Oscar immunity and her mistress's freedom if she surrenders the remaining names. He genuinely believes he is merciful. Beat: temptation dressed as kindness.

chapters.title: The Clock Stops
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Renshaw finds the gatehouse clock; the ledger is gone—Oscar moved it weeks ago, having memorized every name. But Edith is arrested as leverage. Beat: triumph shadowed by guilt.

chapters.title: Letters Never Delivered
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In prison visiting hours, Edith tells Oscar to forget her and save the record. Oscar refuses to choose between them aloud. Beat: love against duty, stated plainly at last.

chapters.title: The Historian's Draft
chapters.summary: New POV: a war-office historian compiling the official account, which erases the women entirely. Oscar reads a leaked proof and understands the true stakes—the ledger was always about the story. Beat: cold clarity.

chapters.title: Every Name, By Heart
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She begins writing the record from memory: names, dates, routes, sacrifices. Nell guards the door; the found family reassembles around the work. Beat: grief transmuted into labor.

chapters.title: The Clerk's Confession
chapters.summary: Clerk Hobbes's POV. Confronted, he breaks—not from threat but from shame—and reveals where seized papers are stored and when they'll be burned. Beat: unexpected mercy toward a betrayer.

chapters.title: Night at the Records Office
chapters.summary: Oscar and Nell's POV. They break in to swap the originals for forgeries before destruction day. Nearly captured; Nell takes a beating covering Oscar's escape. Beat: terror, sacrifice, devotion.

chapters.title: What the Fire Spares
chapters.summary: Renshaw's POV. He burns the forged ledger believing it real, then discovers discrepancies too late. His certainty cracks; he begins keeping his own private record. Beat: the corruptor corrupted by doubt.

chapters.title: Armistice
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The war ends; the occupation dissolves overnight. Edith is released, diminished but unbowed. The town celebrates while Oscar holds the true ledger and wonders who will listen now. Beat: hollow victory, fragile hope.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A public inquiry convenes; Renshaw testifies with careful half-truths. Oscar takes the stand and recites the names from memory, one by one, until the room stops shifting in its seats. Beat: climax—invisibility abandoned, voice claimed.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs briefly. The testimony enters the official transcript ahead of the historians' revision; Edith's name is restored; Renshaw resigns rather than face his own file. Beat: justice partial but real.

chapters.title: A Clock for the Orchard
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, years later. She and Nell keep the orchard together; the repaired gatehouse clock runs again, and schoolchildren visit to hear the story read aloud—from the record, in her own hand. Beat: peace earned, family chosen, time kept.
